section.title: Completeness and the idea of no gaps
section.p: The last section used the real line as if every point on it had a number. That is a stronger promise than it may first appear.
Fractions are already very rich. Between any two fractions there is another fraction. For example, between 1.41 and 1.42 lies
Still, fractions alone leave gaps. Geometry finds one of those gaps in a unit square.

note.title: First-reading note
note.p: This section explains why the real numbers, not only rational numbers, are the right setting for calculus. You may read the proof details lightly on a first pass. The main idea is simple: calculus needs an unbroken number line because limits can point to numbers that no finite decimal or fraction exactly equals.

note.p: Fractions can approximate the diagonal of a unit square as closely as we want, but no fraction equals it.

paragraphs.p: This is the first warning that “many numbers” is not the same as “no gaps.”

exercise.title: Why is many numbers not the same as no gaps?

statement.p: Between any two fractions there is another fraction, yet the diagonal of a unit square still points to a missing rational number. In your own words, what does it mean that fractions can approximate \sqrt2 as closely as we want, and why does that still leave a gap?

hint.p: Approaching a number is not the same as being that number. Ask whether the destination itself has to be a fraction.

note.title: Nested Interval Principle
note.p: is a nested sequence of closed intervals

subsection.p: For the intervals above, that one real number is \sqrt2.

paragraphs.title: Idea of the proof
paragraphs.p: The left endpoints
move to the right or stay fixed. The right endpoints
move to the left or stay fixed. Since every left endpoint is still to the left of every right endpoint, the left endpoints are bounded above.

The real numbers have a least upper bound for the left endpoints. Call it L. Then L lies in every closed interval. If two different numbers x<y lay in every interval, then every interval would have length at least y-x. But the interval lengths become arbitrarily small. Therefore there can be only one such number.
This proof depends on the fact that the left endpoints have a least upper bound. That fact is one form of completeness (absence of holes) of real numbers.

paragraphs.title: What goes wrong with rational numbers
paragraphs.p: Take the same nested intervals, but allow only rational numbers. Each interval contains many rational numbers. Their lengths shrink toward 0. But the only real number common to all of them is \sqrt2, and \sqrt2 is not rational.
So inside the rational numbers alone, these nested rational intervals have no rational point in common.
That is a gap.

statement.p: The decimal approximations to \sqrt2 produce nested closed intervals whose lengths shrink toward 0. In your own words, what does the Nested Interval Principle promise on the real line, and why does the same picture fail if we allow only rational numbers?

hint.p: Each interval contains the next, and the lengths become arbitrarily small. The question is whether a common point is guaranteed to exist inside the number system you are using.

note.title: Maximum versus least upper bound
note.p: A maximum must belong to the set.
A least upper bound may or may not belong to the set.

statement.p: Now we can state the completeness property.

note.title: Completeness Property of the Real Numbers
note.p: Every nonempty set of real numbers that is bounded above has a least upper bound.

statement.p: This property is what fills the gaps. It is not true for the rational numbers.

exercise.title: How is a least upper bound different from a maximum?

statement.p: The open interval (0,1) has least upper bound 1, even though 1 is not in the set. In your own words, what is a least upper bound, and why can a set fail to contain the number that caps it from above?

hint.p: A maximum must belong to the set. A least upper bound is the smallest ceiling, whether or not the set reaches that ceiling.

note.title: What the proof showed
note.p: The existence of \sqrt2 is not a decimal accident. It follows from the no-gaps property of the real numbers.

subsection.title: Why calculus needs the real numbers
subsection.p: Calculus builds exact numbers from limiting processes.

A tangent slope is approached by slopes of secant lines. An area is approached by sums of thin rectangles. A root can be trapped by bisection inside smaller and smaller intervals. An infinite decimal is approached by its finite decimal truncations.
Each step in such a process may use rational numbers. But the number approached may be irrational.
The rational numbers are excellent for computation. They are not complete enough for calculus.

Continuing forever gives nested intervals whose lengths shrink to 0. The real number trapped by this process is \sqrt2. If we allowed only rational numbers, the process would point to a hole.

paragraphs.title: The calculus lesson
paragraphs.p: A limiting process is a promise that approximations have a destination. Completeness says that, for the real line, the destination exists.
We will not mention completeness every time we take a limit. But it is quietly underneath the whole subject. It is what lets the language of “as close as we want” point to an actual number.

The real line gives us numbers and distances. The next step is to let one number determine another. A temperature depends on time. A position depends on time. An error depends on a step size h. Those dependencies are called functions.

exercise.title: Why does a limiting process need an unbroken number line?

statement.p: A tangent slope, an area, a bisection root, and an infinite decimal are all approached by approximations. In your own words, what promise is a limiting process making, and why is completeness the property that lets that destination be an actual real number?

hint.p: Each step of the process may use rational numbers. Completeness is about whether the number being approached is allowed to exist even when it is not rational.
